lead: Some things you're happy to do simply because doing them feels good.
when: When studying is hard to stick with, a hobby has turned into a chore, or you want to help someone else get more actively involved, this is a good place to look.
body:
You lose track of time while drawing, feel satisfied when you crack a tough problem, or grow flowers just because you love watching them slowly come up. These may all involve intrinsic motivation: not doing it for grades, bonuses, or other people's likes, but because the activity itself is worth your time. It explains why you want to keep going with some things even when nobody is pushing you.

In self-determination theory, intrinsic motivation means engaging in an activity for the interest and satisfaction inherent in the activity itself, as distinct from acting for a separable external outcome.

To support this kind of drive, give yourself some choice, make your progress visible, and stay connected with people who support you. The theory sees autonomy, competence, and relatedness as important needs. In plain words: "I get some say," "I can do this, and I'm getting better," and "there are people here who understand me."
example:
You used to love taking photos, then you started running an account, and every time you went out you only thought about which shots would get more likes. Gradually, picking up the camera made you think of numbers and comparisons, and the joy of watching the light faded.

You could set aside some time to shoot only what you want, with no need to post it, and aim your practice at improving a particular skill rather than needing every photo to win. You don't have to dislike outside recognition. Just leave the activity itself some room to breathe, so results don't take over all the fun.
extra: If a child loves drawing and you always ask how they placed in the competition, drawing may slowly become nothing more than "turning in results." Try asking what they drew and which part they like best, paying attention to the exploring, not just the outcome.
steps: Ask yourself whether there's some small part of this that you'd happily do even if nobody knew.
Give it a reasonable amount of choice and small challenges you can complete, and add a bit more difficulty once you see progress.
Look for support and shared interests, and cut down on unnecessary rankings, nagging, and the feeling of being watched.
caution: Having intrinsic interest doesn't mean you don't need rest, and it doesn't mean others can skip paying you fairly. Dull but necessary tasks still need to be divided fairly; they can't be solved just by saying "you should love it."
exercise: For an activity you used to enjoy that now feels stressful, set aside twenty minutes of "no grading" time. Do only the small part that interests you, and notice how it feels different.
brief: The interest loop of the activity itself: a stick figure is absorbed in a geometric puzzle, feels happy after finishing it, and then eagerly tries a new puzzle; a short loop links interest, engagement, and satisfaction.
